input.rationale: The pre-vote-disabled receipt separates the two gates the earlier negative result left entangled, so the account of why uniform configurations keep the separation can now name the gate that does the work instead of the combination. Every trial formed the higher-term candidacy the previous run could not, and no trial produced an overlap, which puts the separation on the peers' known-leader refusal together with their own heartbeat timers and makes pre-vote an additional gate that prevents the candidacy from forming at all. This submission appends that interpretation, corrects the knowledge entry under its existing id with the changed premise and its recorded use, and marks the question answered.

knowledge.statement: Uniformly configured clusters keep a cut-off leader's confirmation window ahead of any competing election, and the gate that does it is the peers' refusal to vote while they still have the leader in view: a node with a known leader rejects a vote request from any other candidate before comparing terms, and that knowledge lapses no earlier than its own heartbeat timer, which ValidateConfig keeps at or above the leader's lease. Pre-vote is a second, additional gate rather than the necessary one: with pre-vote enabled an isolated node never raises its term, and with pre-vote disabled it does raise its term and still cannot collect a vote before the lease expires, which is what the pre-vote-disabled run measured.
knowledge.conditions: Nodes sharing their timer settings; ValidateConfig's per-node relation LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout holding; the candidate isolated from the leader and from a majority of voters. The additional pre-vote gate applies when pre-vote is enabled, which is the captured default.
knowledge.changed_premise: The original statement said two gates keep the separation and that the run could not attribute it to either alone. The pre-vote-disabled run shows the higher-term candidacy forming in every trial while the separation still held, so the statement now distinguishes the gate that produces the separation (a peer that still has the leader in view refuses the vote request before comparing terms, and that view lapses no earlier than the peer's own heartbeat timer, which with shared settings is at least the leader's lease) from the additional gate (with pre-vote enabled the candidacy does not form at all). The behaviour described is a correction of attribution, not of the observations.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 17133140c8064f01b7884e490ec6bc02, exit 0, tests_passed, 52 parsed events, 0 parse errors; twelve hand-built four-node clusters with identical 50ms settings and PreVoteDisabled set on every node). Comparison 0, which predicted that a live higher-term candidacy would let a confirmation overlap a competing election, came back violated and complete, with all twelve trials as valid witnesses: no trial produced a competing leader during the confirmation window and none produced a confirmation after one. The trials nevertheless did produce what they were built to force: preexisting_candidate is true in all twelve, and the isolated voter sat at terms three to five against a leader at two or three, so unlike the previous run a real, higher-term candidacy was alive throughout the window. The confirmations ended at the leader's lease in every trial (47-59ms, seventeen to twenty confirmations each) and the leader stepped down in every trial. Together with the earlier run - where pre-vote kept the isolated voter at the leader's own term - the two receipts separate the gates: pre-vote prevents an isolated node from raising its term at all, and it is the peers' known-leader refusal, released only when their own heartbeat timers expire, that keeps the separation when a candidacy does exist. investigations.question: If a leadership transfer is interrupted while its drain loop still has replication work, can the transfer goroutine be stranded on the followerReplication triggerDeferErrorCh send so that the deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) never runs, leaving a node that later becomes leader permanently rejecting client operations with ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress?
investigations.hypothesis: The drain loop sends a deferError on repl.triggerDeferErrorCh outside any arm on the transfer's stop channel, and the only reader of that channel is the peer's replication goroutine, which exits when the leader steps down (runLeader's defer closes its stopCh) or when the peer is removed. If the leader loses leadership between the goroutine's wake-up and that send, the send has no reader and blocks forever; the outer transfer goroutine then blocks on doneCh before its deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false), so the flag stays set for the lifetime of the Raft instance, including after a later election of that instance.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real three-voter cluster, isolate the transfer target, commit a backlog that the target never receives, start a transfer to that target, then cut the starting leader off so it steps down while the transfer is draining. Predict: the transfer future resolves with an error, the drained goroutine is left in the triggerDeferErrorCh send, getLeadershipTransferInProgress stays true, and after the old leader is made leader again through a normal transfer its Apply and GetConfiguration return ErrLeadershipTransferInProgress. A control trial without the interruption must show the flag cleared and client calls unaffected; if every interrupted trial clears the flag with no stranded goroutine, the hypothesis is defeated for this trigger.

investigations.question: Does VerifyLeader confirm leadership using acknowledgements that do not count toward the voter quorum, so that a leader separated from every other voter but still able to reach a nonvoter reports itself verified?
investigations.hypothesis: verifyLeader seeds votes with the leader's own vote and registers the verify future with every followerReplication in leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication creates for every server in the latest configuration including nonvoters; each successful AppendEntries response then calls notifyAll, which casts a vote for every registered future. Since quorumSize counts only voters, acknowledgements from nonvoters can complete the voter quorum, so a leader whose only reachable peers are nonvoters returns a successful VerifyLeader while it cannot contact a majority of voters - and while another leader may already have been elected among the voters it cannot reach.
investigations.discriminator: Run a real cluster of three voters plus one nonvoter, elect the leader, confirm it can verify normally, then partition the leader together with the nonvoter away from the other two voters and call VerifyLeader on the leader before the new term reaches the nonvoter. Predict: the future returns nil with votes counting only the leader's own vote plus the nonvoter's acknowledgement, while the leader's configurations.latest contains three voters, so the confirmation is made against a quorum of voters it cannot reach; a control in which the nonvoter is also cut off must fail the verification instead.

investigations.question: On a leader that has lost contact with every other voter but can still reach a nonvoter, for how long do verifications keep succeeding relative to the moment the detached voters elect their own leader and commit entries - does the confirmation window overlap a competing leader, or does the leader's own lease end it first?
investigations.hypothesis: Because checkLeaderLease counts only voters, the cut-off leader keeps confirming only until its lease check steps it down, which is one LeaderLeaseTimeout after its last successful contact with a voter; the detached voters' election starts from their own heartbeat timeouts. With the captured relations between those timers the confirmation window may close before a competing leader appears, in which case the defect is confined to the confirmation primitive - an unsound confirmation while no competing leader yet exists - rather than to an observed stale read.
investigations.discriminator: Partition the leader together with the nonvoter on a real three-voter plus one-nonvoter cluster, poll the exported verification path while it is confirmable, record the last successful confirmation's elapsed time, then watch until the detached voters report a leader and record when that happens and whether it precedes or follows the last confirmation. Overlap (a competing leader before the last confirmation) would support a stale-read consequence; a clean separation would narrow it. The control, with the nonvoter cut off too, must produce no confirmations at all.

investigations.question: Does AddVoter install the new server as a Voter immediately, in contrast to its documented staging behaviour, so that adding a server that is not yet running can leave a cluster unable to commit or to elect, and unable to undo the change through the same API?
investigations.hypothesis: AddVoter's comment promises that the server is added as a staging server and promoted once it is ready, but nextConfiguration's AddVoter branch builds the new Server with Suffrage Voter, and Staging is deprecated and unused, so the change takes effect as a full membership change as soon as it is committed. When the number of living voters is below the resulting quorum - for example a single-voter cluster that adds one unreachable server - the leader can no longer contact a quorum, steps down through its lease check, and the cluster has no way back through the API because an election needs the same quorum and config changes require a leader.
investigations.discriminator: Add an address that no transport answers through the exported AddVoter API, on a single-voter cluster and on a three-voter cluster, and record the resulting configuration (the added server's suffrage and the quorum), whether a subsequent apply succeeds, whether any leader exists afterwards, and whether RemoveServer for the added server succeeds. The hypothesis predicts failure of apply and removal with no leader on the single-voter cluster, and unremarkable success on the three-voter cluster where the living voters still satisfy the quorum.

investigations.question: Does the replication retry backoff a leader applies to a failing follower leave that follower without log replication for an unbounded time after it recovers, because the heartbeat path's successes do not clear the replication failure count?
investigations.hypothesis: replicateTo sleeps backoff(failureWait, s.failures, maxFailureScale) before each attempt and counts every transport error or rejected append in s.failures, while the peer's heartbeat goroutine keeps its own separate failure counter and does not touch s.failures, so a follower that recovers after many consecutive failures could wait for the replication backoff rather than being caught up as soon as it is reachable again.

A measurement would partition a follower long enough to accumulate failures, heal it, and time the catch-up against a short-outage control.

knowledge.statement: verifyLeader seeds the tally with the leader's own vote (votes=1) and sets quorumSize from quorumSize(), which counts only voters in the latest configuration (voters/2+1); it then registers the verify future in each followerReplication in leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates from every server in the latest configuration including nonvoters, and triggers a heartbeat on each. Every successful AppendEntries response calls followerReplication.notifyAll, and verifyFuture.vote increments the tally for every registered future regardless of the responding peer's suffrage, so a nonvoter's acknowledgement contributes to a tally that is compared against a voter quorum.
knowledge.conditions: The node is leader; its latest configuration contains at least one nonvoter whose suffrage is Nonvoter; the nonvoter is reachable while a voter majority is not; VerifyLeader (or the same verifyFuture path) is invoked.

knowledge.statement: A leader that can exchange RPCs only with a nonvoter can obtain a successful VerifyLeader: with three voters and one nonvoter the voter quorum is two, the leader contributes its own vote, and the nonvoter's acknowledgement of an AppendEntries heartbeat supplies the second, so the confirmation is satisfied by an acknowledgement from a server that cannot vote and does not establish that the leader can still reach a voter majority.
knowledge.conditions: Same configuration and partition conditions as the behavior entry; the leader has not yet stepped down through its own lease check, which runs on the LeaderLeaseTimeout timer.

knowledge.statement: The AddVoter configuration change installs the requested server with Suffrage Voter in one step: nextConfiguration's AddVoter branch builds the new Server with Suffrage Voter, the resulting configuration is appended as a single LogConfiguration (or the deprecated remove-peer entry below protocol version 2), and the leader applies it to the commitment and to replication immediately after dispatching it. No captured path creates a Staging server or defers promotion, so the suffrage the operation installs contradicts both published descriptions of the operation (the AddVoter doc comment and membership.md, which lists 'AddVoter: server becomes staging unless voter'), while the promotion loop that membership.md describes is separately declared unimplemented in that same document. The code also deprecates the Staging suffrage and notes that the old AddStaging command was in fact AddVoter, and the Promote command can only act on a Staging server, which no path creates.

knowledge.statement: When the configuration change makes the voter quorum exceed the number of living voters, the cluster loses progress and cannot repair itself in band: the leader's lease check finds contact with fewer voters than the quorum, it steps down, no election can complete because the quorum still requires the unreachable server, applies are answered with ErrNotLeader, and RemoveServer for that server is answered with ErrNotLeader so the configuration still lists it. For one added server this happens exactly when the cluster had a single voter; with two or more living voters, adding a voter leaves the quorum satisfiable and the cluster keeps working.
knowledge.conditions: The added server is not running and no transport can reach it; the pre-change cluster was healthy; captured in-memory timers (heartbeat, election and lease all 50ms in this probe).

knowledge.statement: Two gates keep an isolated voter from displacing a leader whose lease is still running when every node shares its timer settings. A node that knows a leader refuses a vote request from any other candidate before it compares terms, so a candidate cannot collect the vote of a peer that still has the leader in view; and with pre-vote enabled the candidate does not raise its term at all while it cannot assemble a majority, because runCandidate's pre-vote phase keeps the node at its current term and only elects for real after the pre-vote is won. Both gates are released by the same event - a peer losing the leader from view when its own heartbeat timer expires - and that timer is reset by the same leader whose lease is expiring, so with shared settings the lease expires no later than the earliest moment at which a vote could be granted.
knowledge.conditions: Pre-vote enabled (the captured default), sending nodes sharing their timer settings, the candidate isolated from the leader and from a majority of voters, and ValidateConfig's per-node relation LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout holding on every node.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account: RestoreCommittedLogs is documented to replay all known-committed logs on disk before NewRaft completes (config.go 243-254), and restoreFromCommittedLogs does exactly that by calling processLogs before runFSM is started (api.go 606 vs 637). processLogs' applyBatch performs a blocking send on fsmMutateCh (raft.go 1306) whose capacity is 128 (api.go 560) while batching entries at MaxAppendEntries (raft.go 1318, 1345-1348), and runFSM (fsm.go 241) is the only reader of that channel anywhere in the package. Therefore the startup replay can only fit 128*MaxAppendEntries FSM-bound entries; past that the constructor cannot complete, and the escape in applyBatch (the shutdownCh arm) is unreachable because the caller has no *Raft to shut down before NewRaft returns. The sizing is inside the documented use case: DefaultConfig pairs MaxAppendEntries=64 with SnapshotThreshold=8192 and a 120s SnapshotInterval, so a node committing more than 8192 entries between snapshot checks - exactly the follower/restart situation the option targets - comes back with a replay window above the bound. The submitted experiment records the retained-execution state of this account (return vs non-return, window census, batch estimate, blocked stack) for five restart-only cases; the account above is a source derivation, not a reading of that run.

knowledge.assertion: Startup replay blocking-sends FSM batches before runFSM is started.
Non-return once FSM-bound window entries exceed 128*MaxAppendEntries.

counterevidence: The option is off by default (config.go 243-254, RestoreCommittedLogs false in DefaultConfig), so a cluster that does not opt into it cannot reach this path; the defect is scoped to that opt-in configuration.

raft.go 1305-1307 also arms a shutdownCh arm, so the blocked send is not unconditionally permanent: it can be released by Shutdown - but only by a caller that already holds the *Raft, which NewRaft has not yet returned, and by nothing internal (NewRaft starts no routines before this call).
An implementation that used an unbounded or larger FSM channel, or started runFSM first, would not show this; the account is specific to this snapshot's ordering and capacity.
limitations: The precise batch/window boundary (window in FSM-bound entries vs 128*MaxAppendEntries) is derived from source; the submitted probe brackets it with observed windows rather than pinning the exact entry count at which the last fitting send is reached.
The startup replay also holds up to 128 batches (each up to MaxAppendEntries commit tuples) in the channel, so memory use grows with MaxAppendEntries; this submission does not measure that.

Whether a node that blocks here can be recovered by an operator (for example via configuration change) is not investigated; the claim is limited to NewRaft not returning and no internal repair being enabled.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check ec81425b7ebc4941ba70f77e78b109fb, exit 0, tests_passed, 14 parsed events, 0 parse errors). Comparison 0 (within-capacity restart returns) evaluated indices 1, 3, 7, 13 and holds with no missing or contradictory observations: every admitted prefix was correlated by identity (case) to its result (0->1, 2->3, 6->7, 12->13), comparison_complete true. Comparison 1 (over-capacity restart does not return) evaluated indices 5, 9, 11 and holds, correlated with prefixes 4, 8, 10. Observed operands: window 4001 with 4000 FSM-bound entries -> 63 batches, returned in 4ms; window 1000/999 -> 16 batches, returned in 0ms; window 8190/8189 -> exactly 128 batches, returned in 4ms; window 8197/8196 -> 129 batches, did not return within 5s; window 12000/11999 -> 188 batches, did not return; window 1001/1000 with MaxAppendEntries=4 -> 250 batches, did not return. The last two pairs are the discriminators that exclude the rival explanations: the MaxAppendEntries=4 case has essentially the same ~1000-entry window as the case that returned in 0ms with 64-entry batches, so what decides the outcome is batches against channel capacity, not window size alone; and the after-snapshot case applies the same 12000 commands against the same stores yet returns in 7ms because the manual snapshot moves last_applied to 12002 and leaves a window of 0. Each non-return case sampled a goroutine that had not returned out of the replay path, with frames at raft.go:1305 (the select-send of a batch inside processLogs' applyBatch), raft.go:1346 (the batched applyBatch call), api.go:753 (restoreFromCommittedLogs' processLogs call) and api.go:606 (NewRaft), i.e. exactly the source-derived send that has no consumer until api.go:637 starts runFSM. The 5s wait is a harness ceiling and is not load-bearing for the claim: the stack shows the goroutine is inside the replay send, and the source shows the only reader of that channel is started later in the same constructor and that the caller cannot call Shutdown because no *Raft has been returned. Together with the source account this makes the non-return a deadlock of the constructor under the stated configuration, so the account is no longer merely conditional; the previous receipt abb2ff0a1f0f449f87fb9b382c8a3fee is superseded on the evidence side by this parsed run, and its parse loss remains recorded.

knowledge.assertion: The startup replay delivers FSM batches by blocking send on fsmMutateCh before runFSM exists; the blocked stacks in this run end at raft.go:1305 inside processLogs' applyBatch, called from raft.go:1346, from api.go:753 (restoreFromCommittedLogs) and api.go:606 (NewRaft).

Non-return tracks ceil(FSM-bound window entries / MaxAppendEntries) against the 128-slot channel: 63 and 16 batches returned in 0-4ms, 128 batches returned, 129 batches, 188 batches and 250 batches (MaxAppendEntries=4) did not return.

counterevidence: The feature is opt-in: RestoreCommittedLogs defaults to false (config.go 243-254, DefaultConfig), so a cluster that never enables it cannot reach this path; the defect is scoped to that configuration plus a commit-tracking log store.

The blocked send is inside a select with a shutdownCh arm, so it is not unconditional: Shutdown releases it - but only a caller holding the *Raft can call Shutdown, and in the affected path NewRaft has not returned yet, while NewRaft starts no internal routine before this call, so no participant exists that could take that arm during the window.

The probe constructs the large windows by disabling automatic snapshotting; a deployment that snapshots often keeps the window small, so the observed non-returns are not evidence that ordinary clusters of this kind restart broken - only that the constructor cannot complete when the window is large.

For the within-capacity cases the returns were immediate (0-7ms), but a returning restart is only bounded by the harness wait; nothing here claims a bound on restart duration for other configurations.
limitations: Configuration space is sampled, not exhausted: MaxAppendEntries was exercised at 4 and 64 while ValidateConfig allows up to 1024, and the relation tested is the batch count against capacity, so untested settings are covered by the relation rather than by direct observation.

The probe runs a single-voter cluster with an in-memory transport, an in-memory commit-tracking log store and MockFSM, so disk latency, network behaviour and slow FSM application are excluded; a slow FSM would fill the same channel sooner, which limits the observed non-returns as a lower bound rather than an upper one.

The probe does not measure the memory held by the queued batches (up to 128 batches of up to MaxAppendEntries commit tuples), nor whether an operator can recover a node blocked in NewRaft, and no claim is made about either.

The window-to-FSM-bound offset varied by one entry between runs (the persisted commit index is staged with the last StoreLogs), so the exact counts 8189/8196 are specific to these runs; the tested predicate is the batch count against the 128-slot capacity.

Restart outcome is recorded as returned / not returned within 5s with a sampled stack; no attempt is made to force completion or to establish that no future internal or external event could ever release the send beyond the source argument that none is enabled.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 4ad6471fdd1547f28bc88a8f911e0319, exit 0, tests_passed, 6 parsed events, 0 parse errors, snapshot settings reported per case as SnapshotThreshold 8192, SnapshotInterval 120000ms, MaxAppendEntries 64). Comparison 0 (within-capacity restart returns) evaluated result index 5, correlated to admission index 4, and holds; comparison 1 (over-capacity restart does not return) evaluated result indices 1 and 3, correlated to admission indices 0 and 2, and holds. Both are comparison_complete with no missing or contradictory observations, and neither result was filtered on the measured field: applicability came from replay_batches_within_capacity, which is decided by the pre-restart operands carried in the admission event. Observed state: with no snapshot at all, persisted commit index 10001 above last-applied 0 gives a window of 10001 entries (10000 FSM-bound, 157 batches) and NewRaft had not returned after 5s; with a real user snapshot at index 4002 followed by 9998 more commits, the window is 9998 (157 batches) and NewRaft had not returned; with the same snapshot followed by only 1999 commits, the window is 1999 (32 batches) and NewRaft returned in 7ms. Each non-return sampled a goroutine still inside the replay path (raft.go:1305 inside the batch select-send, raft.go:1346, api.go:753 restoreFromCommittedLogs, api.go:606 NewRaft). The applicability question is therefore answered from the target's own behaviour: the periodic snapshot does not cap the window below the 128-batch bound. The mechanism is that runSnapshots consults shouldSnapshot only on the SnapshotInterval timer (snapshot.go 73-100), shouldSnapshot compares the log-store last index against the last snapshot index (snapshot.go 107-120), and the startup replay window is measured from the newest snapshot to the persisted commit index, so between checks the window is simply however many committed entries accumulated, and before the first check it is the whole committed log. With the captured defaults that accumulation exceeds 8192 FSM-bound entries whenever more than about 8192 commits occur per 120s interval, i.e. above roughly 68 commits/s sustained, at which point the window at an arbitrary restart exceeds the 128*64 = 8192 bound and NewRaft cannot complete. The third counterevidence recorded in the previous revision (windows only constructed by disabling automatic snapshotting) is answered by this receipt and no longer stands; the remaining counterevidence is listed below.

0d83a8cdded948c3b78d936f719d97d7-gap-0.explanation: Answered from the retained execution: with the captured snapshot settings in force (threshold 8192, interval 120s, both reported in the admission events) a node reaches a restart whose window exceeds the bound - 10001 entries / 157 batches with no snapshot yet taken, and 9998 / 157 after a real snapshot at 4002 plus 9998 more commits - and both restarts fail to return, while the 1999-entry control returns in 7ms. Source reading explains why the periodic check cannot prevent this: the check runs only on the SnapshotInterval timer (snapshot.go 73-100), its condition is a last-index minus last-snapshot delta against SnapshotThreshold (snapshot.go 107-120), and the replay window is measured from the newest snapshot to the persisted commit index, so the window is whatever accumulated since the newest snapshot. The residual condition is a rate premise rather than a target property: with the defaults the window exceeds 8192 FSM-bound entries when more than about 8192 commits occur per 120s interval (about 68/s sustained), and a sufficiently small SnapshotInterval relative to the write rate keeps the window below the bound.

knowledge.assertion: In this run too the non-returning goroutine's frames are raft.go:1305 (batch select-send in processLogs' applyBatch), raft.go:1346, api.go:753 (restoreFromCommittedLogs) and api.go:606 (NewRaft), with the only reader of fsmMutateCh started later at api.go:637.
With the configured snapshot settings in force, windows of 10001 and 9998 FSM-bound entries (157 batches each) did not return, while 1999 entries (32 batches) returned in 7ms.

counterevidence: The feature remains opt-in: RestoreCommittedLogs defaults to false and requires a CommitTrackingLogStore, so a cluster that does not enable it cannot reach this path.

The blocked send has a shutdownCh arm, so it is releasable by Shutdown - but the affected caller holds no *Raft because NewRaft has not returned, and NewRaft starts no routine before the replay, so nothing can take that arm during the window.

Scope-narrowing premise: the deadlock needs the window above the bound at the restart, which with the captured defaults requires a sustained commit rate of roughly 68 commits/s or more between snapshot checks (or a configuration that raises SnapshotThreshold, lengthens SnapshotInterval, or prevents snapshots from being taken); below that rate the periodic snapshot keeps the window small and the constructor returns.
limitations: No full 120s interval elapsed in the probe: the accumulation is produced by the target's own apply path rather than by wall-clock passage, so the rate at which the same accumulation occurs in time is arithmetic on the configured interval, not an observation.

The newest snapshot in the two snapshot cases is placed by a user snapshot at a chosen index; with automatic snapshots the placement is at an interval tick, which changes the phase of the accumulation but not its bound, and that equivalence is a source argument rather than an observation.

The probe still runs a single-voter cluster with an in-memory transport, an in-memory commit-tracking store and MockFSM, so disk latency, network behaviour and slow FSM application are excluded; MaxAppendEntries is the configured default here and was varied only in the predecessor experiment.
Unchanged from earlier: the memory held by queued batches is not measured, and whether an operator can recover a node blocked inside NewRaft is not investigated.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 991fd67c1e3d4760b83fd8a724444ff0, exit 0, tests_passed, 12 parsed events, 0 parse errors) plus the source reading that the run's outcome matches. The probe did exercise the intended state: in every interrupted trial the target's last index at transfer time was 2 against the leader's 202, so the drain loop had real replication work after the target was isolated, and each transfer future resolved with 'leadership transfer timeout' rather than completing, i.e. the transfer was still in flight when the starting leader was cut off and its replication goroutine exited. Against the hypothesis's prediction, in all ten interrupted trials transfer_in_progress_after was false, no goroutine was found stranded in the leadershipTransfer/triggerDeferErrorCh path, and in the three trials where another node became leader first the interrupted node was re-elected and its Apply and GetConfiguration both succeeded with no error; the two uninterrupted controls completed with an empty transfer error, the starting node ending as Follower with the flag false. The source reason, which is the primary basis for refutation: followerReplication.triggerDeferErrorCh is created with capacity 1 (raft.go 603), and leadershipTransfer only reaches its next send (raft.go 1003) after receiving the response for the previous deferError, which by construction means the replicator consumed that item, so the buffer is empty at each send and a buffered send succeeds without any reader. A send cannot therefore be stranded by the replicator exiting, and the outer goroutine's wait on doneCh is always satisfied, so the deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) runs - which is what every trial shows. The alternative interleaving-theoretical reading is also excluded empirically across two scheduling regimes: the ten retained trials on the host's default parallelism plus six additional local trials with GOMAXPROCS=1, which should favour the single-threaded ordering the hypothesis needed, all cleared the flag with no stranded goroutine; the GOMAXPROCS run is native feedback and is not offered as retained evidence.
counterevidence: The refutation is about reachability through this trigger, not about the flag's design: setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) really is only reached from the outer transfer goroutine's deferred call, so any exit path of the inner goroutine that skips doneCh would still leave the flag set. The probe's trials exercised the drain-in-flight interruption, the timeout and the leadership-loss paths, but not a state where the transport call itself never returns.

The stranded-goroutine search is a sampled goroutine dump at one instant per trial; it would miss a goroutine that had already exited, but the primary basis does not depend on the dump - the buffered send cannot block regardless of sampling.
limitations: Timings are the captured in-memory ones (50ms heartbeat, election and lease), and the transfer therefore timed out before the target could win; different timing would change which branch resolves the transfer, though not the buffered-send argument.
Three of ten interrupted trials reached the re-election check; the other seven had no other leader within the 3s wait, so the client-endpoint check was exercised three times, not ten.

interpretations.rationale: Answered from source and from the transfer receipts rather than by new injection. The handler does validate nothing: raft.timeoutNow (raft.go 2232-2237) ignores the request's origin and any term, because TimeoutNowRequest carries only the RPC header (commands.go 206-208), and it immediately clears the leader, moves the node to Candidate and marks the candidacy as transfer-driven, which makes its RequestVote waive the known-leader rejection on other servers. What the question turned on, however, is whether a TimeoutNow that no longer reflects the current leader can be produced inside the library. The producer is the leadership-transfer path, and it reaches trans.TimeoutNow (raft.go 1026) only after its drain loop exits, which requires the target to be caught up; the loop's exit and the send are adjacent statements with no blocking point between them, and every earlier exit point of the loop is guarded by the transfer's stop channel (raft.go 1000-1020), which the transfer case closes when leadership is lost or the transfer times out. The interrupted-transfer receipt shows the same shape from the behaviour side: with real replication work pending, the transfer either times out with the flag cleared or is abandoned on leadership loss, and no message was produced after leadership was gone. External injection of a TimeoutNow is not evidence of a target defect here, because peer authentication is the transport's and application's responsibility rather than a guarantee of this library. So the suspicion is refuted for internal producers, and what remains is a hardening observation: the handler would be more defensive if the request carried the sender's term, or if the receiver checked that the sender is its current leader.
counterevidence: The window between the drain loop's exit and the TimeoutNow call is adjacent code rather than a proven impossibility: a preemption exactly there, or a future change that inserts work between them, would reopen it. Nothing in the source prevents that window from existing, only from being wide or reachable in the tested flows.

The vote bypass that the transfer flag enables is intentional and is what makes a transfer target electable while peers still know the old leader; the refutation is about the absence of a stale internal producer, not about the bypass being wrong.
limitations: This answer rests on source reading of the producer path plus the interrupted-transfer executions; no execution produced a transfer message after leadership was lost, so the refutation is a reachability argument with corroborating runs, not a proof about every scheduler.
A cluster whose transport reports delayed or replayed RPCs is outside what these runs cover; the question was scoped to producers inside this snapshot.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 740c189c24af4a62b301aaa2281d8f62, exit 0, tests_passed, 5 parsed events, 0 parse errors, run on a real four-voter cluster with one voter demoted to nonvoter via DemoteVoter, so three voters plus one nonvoter and a voter quorum of two). Comparison 0 holds and is complete on result index 1, admitted by its own baseline at index 0: after the leader was partitioned together with the nonvoter, VerifyLeader returned success with votes 2 against quorum 2 while the leader state was still Leader. Comparison 1 holds and is complete on result index 4, admitted by the baseline at index 3: the same leader, with no peer on its side of the partition, ended with votes 1 against quorum 2 and the verification failed with 'leadership lost while committing log'. The two results differ only in whether a nonvoter sat on the leader's side of the partition, and the tally difference (2 versus 1) is exactly one acknowledgement, which is the nonvoter's: that is the mechanism claim, and it is also what the source says, since quorumSize counts only voters while notifyAll increments the tally for every registered followerReplication, and startStopReplication creates one for nonvoters as well. Comparison 2 - that the voters the leader could not reach elected their own leader and committed an entry above the interrupted leader's applied index while the leader held that successful verification - returned unknown, and the reason is my own admission scoping rather than the target or the observation: the shared prerequisite alias admitted both trials' baseline events, and the control trial deliberately emits no peer-side event, so missing_indices contains the control's baseline at index 3 and comparison_complete is false. The retained peer-side event at index 2 does carry the operands (new_leader_elected true, write_committed true, write_index 6, leader_applied_index 4, leader_applied_lags_new_commit true) and they are attached to this receipt, but because the declared comparison did not complete over them they are reported here as an observation rather than as a held comparison, and the corrected successor is submitted for a fresh execution. The mechanism half of the defect is therefore asserted on a complete, admitted comparison with its control; the consequence half is pending that successor.
counterevidence: At the moment of the successful confirmation the interrupted leader is still the legitimate leader of its term and has not yet exceeded its own leader lease, so one could argue the confirmation is temporally accurate; the defect is that the confirmation cannot distinguish a leader that can still reach a voter majority from one that cannot, which is precisely the question the documented read path uses VerifyLeader to answer, and the leader's own lease is a timer rather than a per-call check.

The control failed through the leader's lease step-down (ErrLeadershipLost), not through an immediate negative acknowledgement, so the pair differs in how it fails as well as in the tally; the directly comparable operand is the tally itself (2 versus 1) against the same quorum of 2.
A deployment without nonvoters cannot reach this path, since the extra acknowledgement has to come from a server whose Suffrage is not Voter.
limitations: The reachability premise is a property of the partition the harness applied, reported as the leader-side suffrages, and is corroborated by the detached voters electing their own leader; the contact-timestamp operand in the same events still reflects pre-partition contact and is not used as evidence of reachability.

One configuration was tested (three voters, one nonvoter, quorum two) with the captured in-memory timeouts; the arithmetic generalizes to any configuration with a nonvoter, but only this one was observed.

The comparison of the interrupted leader's applied index against the newer commit was retained as an observation only, because its declared comparison was incomplete for the reason above; the successor's receipt will decide it.

Comparison 1 holds and is complete on result index 4, admitted by the control baseline at index 3: the same leader with no peer on its side ended with votes 1 against quorum 2 and the verification failed with 'leadership lost while committing log'. Comparison 2 holds and is complete on result index 2, admitted by the interrupted-case baseline through the corrected alias: new_leader_elected true, write_committed true, write_index 6, leader_applied_index 4, so an entry committed by the voters the interrupted leader could not reach sits above the interrupted leader's applied index while that leader was holding its successful confirmation. Read together, the three say: the confirmation that the documented read path uses to avoid stale data was satisfied by one acknowledgement from a server that cannot vote (votes 2 against a quorum of 2), the control shows the same leader without that acknowledgement fails the same call, and the majority the leader could not reach went on to elect a leader and commit an index the confirmed leader never applied. That is a sourced defect in the confirmation contract rather than an execution artefact: quorumSize counts only voters while notifyAll increments the tally for every registered followerReplication and startStopReplication creates one per server including nonvoters, so the tally and the quorum are measured over different populations. The predecessor receipt 740c189c24af4a62b301aaa2281d8f62 remains valid for comparisons 0 and 1 and is superseded only in that its third comparison was incomplete for a harness admission reason that this run removes; the same harness bytes produced both runs.

knowledge.assertion: The tally is incremented for every registered followerReplication, including the one created for a nonvoter, while the compared quorum counts only voters.
With three voters and one reachable nonvoter a leader cut off from the other voters is confirmed with tally 2 against quorum 2.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only answer, no execution. The suspicion is defeated by the arithmetic of the backoff: util.go's backoff doubles failureWait only while the round number is above two and never beyond limit, so with failureWait 10ms and maxFailureScale 12 the ceiling is 10ms*2^10, about 10.24s, and it cannot grow further no matter how long the follower stays unreachable. The count that feeds it is cleared in the same function that uses it: a successful append clears s.failures, and a rejected append that asks for older logs with NoRetryBackoff set clears it as well, so the first attempt that reaches a recovered follower resets the penalty. The heartbeat goroutine's separate counter and its own capped backoff matter for the leader's lease and for verifications, not for this, and the two paths cannot disagree indefinitely because the replication attempt itself is what clears the penalty. What remains is a bounded delay of at most one backoff interval after a long outage - a deliberate curtailment of retry rate rather than a stall - and the correct reading is that the leader resumes replication to a recovered follower within that bound, not that the follower is stranded.
counterevidence: The bound is a delay, not zero: after roughly twelve consecutive failures the leader does wait about ten seconds between attempts, and if a quorum depends on that follower then commits wait with it; the refutation is about unboundedness, not about the delay existing.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only revision that closes the phase limitation of the previous account; the twelve-trial receipt and its operands are unchanged and remain the measured basis. The question was whether a partition landing while a follower is already campaigning could put a competing leader in place before the cut-off leader's confirmations stop. Two gates in the follower path answer it. First, a node that knows a leader refuses a vote request from any other candidate before it looks at terms at all, so a pre-existing candidate cannot collect the vote of a peer that still has the leader in view, and that peer only clears its view and starts its own campaign when its heartbeat timer fires, having been reset by the same leader whose lease is expiring. Second, ValidateConfig enforces LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout per node, so for a cluster that shares its settings the cut-off leader's lease expires no later than the earliest moment any peer can begin campaigning, and the peer then also needs a full election round before a new leader exists. That is the same ordering the twelve trials measured (last confirmations 44-49ms, competing leaders 67-142ms) and it explains it mechanically rather than falling out of scheduling: the confirmation window closes first because the leader's own lease check is the earliest event in the sequence, and the leader's lease check counts voters only, which is why the reachable nonvoter prolongs confirmation without prolonging leadership. The consequence of the parent finding is therefore bounded for uniform configurations, and the unsound confirmation remains the surviving defect. The exception is a cluster whose nodes do not share settings: a follower configured with a heartbeat timeout shorter than the leader's leader-lease timeout could begin an election first, and the relation is enforced per node rather than across the cluster. Nothing in the captured defaults produces that, a mixed configuration is what would, and this run did not construct one.
counterevidence: The mixed-timing exception is not merely theoretical to the extent that rollouts leave nodes with different settings and the library validates each node independently; it is unmeasured here, and it is the one configuration in which the confirmation window and a competing leader could overlap.

The gating argument assumes peers evaluate the vote request as recorded in the snapshot's requestVote path, including the transfer-flagged bypass; a transfer-derived request waives the known-leader gate, which is the mechanism examined and refuted in the sibling question for internal producers.
No application read is served in these runs, so even an overlap would only be a missing basis for a consistent read rather than an observed stale result.
limitations: This revision is a source argument appended to a measured account; it does not add an execution, and the twelve-trial receipt remains the observed evidence.
The mixed-timing case is identified rather than tested; constructing it would need per-node configurations, which the cluster helper used here does not provide.
The reasoning covers the two gates named above and not every possible way a candidate could gain a vote, for example a peer that has never heard of the leader because it joined afterwards.

investigations.question: Does the replication retry backoff a leader applies to a failing follower leave that follower without log replication for an unbounded time after it recovers, because the heartbeat path's successes do not clear the replication failure count?

knowledge.statement: For the startup replay, non-return of NewRaft follows from the size of the replay window: with W FSM-bound entries (LogCommand, LogBarrier and LogConfiguration above protocol version 2, per prepareLog) delivered in ceil(W/MaxAppendEntries) batches against a 128-slot fsmMutateCh, the send only fits while ceil(W/MaxAppendEntries) <= 128. Every successful AppendEntries response calls followerReplication.notifyAll, and verifyFuture.vote increments the tally for every registered future regardless of the responding peer's suffrage, so a nonvoter's acknowledgement contributes to a tally that is compared against a voter quorum.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account: RestoreCommittedLogs is documented to replay all known-committed logs on disk before NewRaft completes (config.go 243-254), and restoreFromCommittedLogs does exactly that by calling processLogs before runFSM is started (api.go 606 vs 637). processLogs' applyBatch performs a blocking send on fsmMutateCh (raft.go 1306) whose capacity is 128 (api.go 560) while batching entries at MaxAppendEntries (raft.go 1318, 1345-1348), and runFSM (fsm.go 241) is the only reader of that channel anywhere in the package. Therefore the startup replay can only fit 128*MaxAppendEntries FSM-bound entries; past that the constructor cannot complete, and the escape in applyBatch (the shutdownCh arm) is unreachable because the caller has no *Raft to shut down before NewRaft returns. The sizing is inside the documented use case: DefaultConfig pairs MaxAppendEntries=64 with SnapshotThreshold=8192 and a 120s SnapshotInterval, so a node committing more than 8192 entries between snapshot checks - exactly the follower/restart situation the option targets - comes back with a replay window above the bound. The submitted experiment records the retained-execution state of this account (return vs non-return, window census, batch estimate, blocked stack) for five restart-only cases; the account above is a source derivation, not a reading of that run.

knowledge.assertion: Startup replay blocking-sends FSM batches before runFSM is started.
Non-return once FSM-bound window entries exceed 128*MaxAppendEntries.

counterevidence: The option is off by default (config.go 243-254, RestoreCommittedLogs false in DefaultConfig), so a cluster that does not opt into it cannot reach this path; the defect is scoped to that opt-in configuration.

raft.go 1305-1307 also arms a shutdownCh arm, so the blocked send is not unconditionally permanent: it can be released by Shutdown - but only by a caller that already holds the *Raft, which NewRaft has not yet returned, and by nothing internal (NewRaft starts no routines before this call).
An implementation that used an unbounded or larger FSM channel, or started runFSM first, would not show this; the account is specific to this snapshot's ordering and capacity.
limitations: The precise batch/window boundary (window in FSM-bound entries vs 128*MaxAppendEntries) is derived from source; the submitted probe brackets it with observed windows rather than pinning the exact entry count at which the last fitting send is reached.
The startup replay also holds up to 128 batches (each up to MaxAppendEntries commit tuples) in the channel, so memory use grows with MaxAppendEntries; this submission does not measure that.

Whether a node that blocks here can be recovered by an operator (for example via configuration change) is not investigated; the claim is limited to NewRaft not returning and no internal repair being enabled.

interpretations.rationale: Retained execution (check 991fd67c1e3d4760b83fd8a724444ff0, exit 0, tests_passed, 12 parsed events, 0 parse errors) plus the source reading that the run's outcome matches. A send cannot therefore be stranded by the replicator exiting, and the outer goroutine's wait on doneCh is always satisfied, so the deferred setLeadershipTransferInProgress(false) runs - which is what every trial shows. The probe's trials exercised the drain-in-flight interruption, the timeout and the leadership-loss paths, but not a state where the transport call itself never returns.

The stranded-goroutine search is a sampled goroutine dump at one instant per trial; it would miss a goroutine that had already exited, but the primary basis does not depend on the dump - the buffered send cannot block regardless of sampling.

interpretations.rationale: Answered from source and from the transfer receipts rather than by new injection. The handler does validate nothing: raft.timeoutNow (raft.go 2232-2237) ignores the request's origin and any term, because TimeoutNowRequest carries only the RPC header (commands.go 206-208), and it immediately clears the leader, moves the node to Candidate and marks the candidacy as transfer-driven, which makes its RequestVote waive the known-leader rejection on other servers. What the question turned on, however, is whether a TimeoutNow that no longer reflects the current leader can be produced inside the library. The producer is the leadership-transfer path, and it reaches trans.TimeoutNow (raft.go 1026) only after its drain loop exits, which requires the target to be caught up; the loop's exit and the send are adjacent statements with no blocking point between them, and every earlier exit point of the loop is guarded by the transfer's stop channel (raft.go 1000-1020), which the transfer case closes when leadership is lost or the transfer times out. The interrupted-transfer receipt shows the same shape from the behaviour side: with real replication work pending, the transfer either times out with the flag cleared or is abandoned on leadership loss, and no message was produced after leadership was gone. External injection of a TimeoutNow is not evidence of a target defect here, because peer authentication is the transport's and application's responsibility rather than a guarantee of this library. So the suspicion is refuted for internal producers, and what remains is a hardening observation: the handler would be more defensive if the request carried the sender's term, or if the receiver checked that the sender is its current leader.
counterevidence: The window between the drain loop's exit and the TimeoutNow call is adjacent code rather than a proven impossibility: a preemption exactly there, or a future change that inserts work between them, would reopen it. Nothing in the source prevents that window from existing, only from being wide or reachable in the tested flows.

The vote bypass that the transfer flag enables is intentional and is what makes a transfer target electable while peers still know the old leader; the refutation is about the absence of a stale internal producer, not about the bypass being wrong.
limitations: This answer rests on source reading of the producer path plus the interrupted-transfer executions; no execution produced a transfer message after leadership was lost, so the refutation is a reachability argument with corroborating runs, not a proof about every scheduler.
A cluster whose transport reports delayed or replayed RPCs is outside what these runs cover; the question was scoped to producers inside this snapshot.

interpretations.rationale: Revision of this question's account with the repeated measurement. The suspicion is defeated by the arithmetic of the backoff: util.go's backoff doubles failureWait only while the round number is above two and never beyond limit, so with failureWait 10ms and maxFailureScale 12 the ceiling is 10ms*2^10, about 10.24s, and it cannot grow further no matter how long the follower stays unreachable. The count that feeds it is cleared in the same function that uses it: a successful append clears s.failures, and a rejected append that asks for older logs with NoRetryBackoff set clears it as well, so the first attempt that reaches a recovered follower resets the penalty. The heartbeat goroutine's separate counter and its own capped backoff matter for the leader's lease and for verifications, not for this, and the two paths cannot disagree indefinitely because the replication attempt itself is what clears the penalty. What remains is a bounded delay of at most one backoff interval after a long outage - a deliberate curtailment of retry rate rather than a stall - and the correct reading is that the leader resumes replication to a recovered follower within that bound, not that the follower is stranded.
counterevidence: The bound is a delay, not zero: after roughly twelve consecutive failures the leader does wait about ten seconds between attempts, and if a quorum depends on that follower then commits wait with it; the refutation is about unboundedness, not about the delay existing.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only revision that closes the phase limitation of the previous account; the twelve-trial receipt and its operands are unchanged and remain the measured basis. The question was whether a partition landing while a follower is already campaigning could put a competing leader in place before the cut-off leader's confirmations stop. Two gates in the follower path answer it. First, a node that knows a leader refuses a vote request from any other candidate before it looks at terms at all, so a pre-existing candidate cannot collect the vote of a peer that still has the leader in view, and that peer only clears its view and starts its own campaign when its heartbeat timer fires, having been reset by the same leader whose lease is expiring. Second, ValidateConfig enforces LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout per node, so for a cluster that shares its settings the cut-off leader's lease expires no later than the earliest moment any peer can begin campaigning, and the peer then also needs a full election round before a new leader exists. That is the same ordering the twelve trials measured (last confirmations 44-49ms, competing leaders 67-142ms) and it explains it mechanically rather than falling out of scheduling: the confirmation window closes first because the leader's own lease check is the earliest event in the sequence, and the leader's lease check counts voters only, which is why the reachable nonvoter prolongs confirmation without prolonging leadership. The consequence of the parent finding is therefore bounded for uniform configurations, and the unsound confirmation remains the surviving defect. The exception is a cluster whose nodes do not share settings: a follower configured with a heartbeat timeout shorter than the leader's leader-lease timeout could begin an election first, and the relation is enforced per node rather than across the cluster. Nothing in the captured defaults produces that, a mixed configuration is what would, and this run did not construct one.
counterevidence: The mixed-timing exception is not merely theoretical to the extent that rollouts leave nodes with different settings and the library validates each node independently; it is unmeasured here, and it is the one configuration in which the confirmation window and a competing leader could overlap.
